title: The Cross Against the Wisdom of the World
sum: Paul greets the church in Corinth, together with Sosthenes, and gives thanks for the grace and gifts God has given it (1:1-9). Then he turns to the news from Chloe's people: the church is saying "I belong to Paul," "I belong to Apollos," "I belong to Cephas," "I belong to Christ." He asks, "Has Christ been split into parts?" and says he is glad he baptized so few (1:10-17).

The rest of the chapter is the first great argument of the letter. The message of the cross looks like foolishness to those who are perishing, but it is the power of God to those being saved (1:18-25). Jews want signs, Greeks want wisdom, and Paul preaches a crucified Messiah. The Corinthians themselves prove the point: few of them were wise, powerful or well-born, and God chose what the world despised so that no one may boast except in the Lord (1:26-31).
readings: The chapter answers a report about a divided church. The slogans of 1:12 show rivalry among followers of different teachers, and Paul's reply is to remove the ground of the rivalry: the teachers are servants, and the message they serve is a crucified Christ. This reading keeps the letter close to Chloe's report and the social setting of Corinth.
Read as a theology of the cross
The chapter is one of the New Testament's central statements that God works through weakness. Here the cross is not a lesson added to Christian teaching but the way God defines wisdom and power.

views.H: Corinth was a Roman colony, refounded in 44 BC and full of freed slaves and traders who rose by money. Public speakers were admired and could make a living by performance. A church there inherited the habits of patronage, rank and boasting, and the slogans of 1:12 look like people attaching themselves to a speaker's name as people did in the cities' philosophical schools. The people Paul names, Chloe, Crispus, Gaius and Stephanas, show a church that met in several households. Gallio, the Roman governor before whom Paul was brought (Acts 18:12), is named in a letter of the emperor Claudius found at Delphi and dated to AD 52.
views.C: Chapter 1 contains the clearest picture in the letter of how Paul learned of the problems: the report of Chloe's people (1:11), as distinct from the letter the Corinthians sent (7:1). Scholars disagree whether the four slogans name real parties (F. C. Baur, who reduced them to two groups) or a looser pattern of loyalty to teachers (many recent commentators). Textually, 1:15 has two readings, "you were baptized" and "I baptized", and the Plain English Translation follows the first. Some partition theories divide 1 Corinthians into several letters, but most scholars keep chapters 1-4 together with the rest.
views.L: Verses 1:10-17 are the opening appeal of the whole letter, and Margaret Mitchell reads the whole letter as an appeal for unity that begins here. Verses 1:18-31 run on the contrast of wisdom and foolishness, strength and weakness, with a ring of quotations from Isaiah (1:19), then Jeremiah (1:31). Notice the repeated words "wisdom" (sophia, 15 times in 1:17-2:13), "boast" and "call" (1:2, 9, 24, 26). The chapter begins with the Corinthians being "called" and ends with the reason: "so that no flesh may boast before God."
views.J: A Jewish reader would hear the two Scripture quotations as God's own judgment on human pride: Isaiah 29:14 against Judah's wise, and Jeremiah 9:23-24 against anyone who boasts in wisdom, strength or riches. The "stumbling block" for Jews is a crucified Messiah, which the Torah calls cursed (Deuteronomy 21:23). Paul writes as a Jew to a mostly Gentile church, and his argument is built on Israel's Scripture, which he assumes the Corinthians know. See the note on 1:23.
views.T: Chrysostom preached a series of homilies on 1 Corinthians in the fourth century. Calvin reads 1:21-25 as beating down the presumption of human wisdom (commentary on 1:25). The Orthodox honor "fools for Christ's sake" (see 4:10). Churches differ on what unity in 1:10 requires (the card).

deep.h: What the cross meant in Corinth
deep.b:
To a first-century Roman, crucifixion was the death of slaves and rebels. Cicero said the very word "cross" should be kept from a Roman citizen's body and from his thoughts, eyes and ears (Pro Rabirio 16). Martin Hengel gathered the ancient evidence for how shameful it was. For Jews there was a second problem: the Torah says a man who is hanged is "cursed by God" (Deuteronomy 21:23), and Paul himself says Christ bought us free from the curse of the law, "having become a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13). To preach that God's Messiah and Lord died this way was to offend both sides: "a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles" (1:23).

Paul does not soften the offense. He makes it the test of what counts as wisdom and power. "Christ crucified" is, for those who are called, "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1:24). The claim is not that the cross is irrational. It is that God's way of saving cannot be reached by the means that people use to seek wisdom, which is why the Corinthians' pride in their wisdom is misplaced.

Paul says Christ sent him "not in the wisdom of words" (1:17). That phrase has been read in three ways. Some, such as Duane Litfin, think Paul turned away from the orator's art of winning an audience by skill and chose plain proclamation. Others, such as Bruce Winter, put the phrase in the setting of Corinth's traveling sophists, who competed for pupils and fame, and think Paul refuses that contest. A third reading, such as Stephen Pogoloff's, ties the matter to social status: Corinthians raised their standing by siding with rhetorical teachers, and Paul rejects that use of speech. These readings are not mutually exclusive. What matters for 1:17 is the purpose clause: "so that the cross of Christ would not be made empty."

deep.title: Claude's theory: the "parties" may have been house gatherings
deep.b: Paul names three households he baptized himself (Crispus, Gaius, Stephanas, 1:14-16) and a fourth source, Chloe's people (1:11). The church met in homes (Romans 16:23). It may be that each "slogan" started as loyalty to the household or host who brought a teacher in, so that "I belong to Apollos" meant, in effect, "I meet where Apollos was welcomed." This would fit the Roman habit of patronage and would explain why Paul speaks of belonging (the genitive) rather than agreeing with a teaching. This is my own suggestion. It is close to ideas in Theissen's study of the social setting of the Corinthian church, but I have not seen it argued exactly this way, and the text does not say it.

echoes: Isaiah 29:14; Isaiah 33:18; Jeremiah 9:23-24; Deuteronomy 21:23; Psalm 24:7-10; Romans 1:16; Romans 4:17; Galatians 3:13; Acts 18:1-18; Acts 18:24-28; Proverbs 8:22-31; Wisdom of Solomon 7:25

settings.to: The church of God in Corinth, "called as saints", and all who call on the name of the Lord everywhere
settings.when: At the start of a letter written from Ephesus, in the 50s AD, after Paul had heard from Chloe's people and received the Corinthians' own letter
settings.why: To claim his authority as an apostle, to remind the Corinthians of what God has given them (speech, knowledge, gifts), and to turn their eyes to the day of Christ. A Greek letter opened with thanks to the gods; Paul's thanks prepares for the corrections that follow.
settings.readers: A church that prided itself on its gifts. The thanks is sincere and it is also the first step of the argument: the gifts are grace, not their own achievement.

settings.to: The Corinthian believers as a group, "my brothers", addressed after the report of Chloe's people
settings.when: In answer to news of quarrels among them, who each claimed a teacher
settings.why: To end the rivalry by asking what the leaders actually did: Christ was not divided, Paul was not crucified for them, and they were not baptized into his name. Paul states his mission as telling the good news, not baptizing, and not in clever speech.
settings.readers: Members of a Roman colony used to patrons and rivals. In their world, to "belong to" a speaker or patron was a social badge. Paul tells them that badge has no place in the church.
views: F. C. Baur read the slogans as standing for two real groups: a Petrine party (which took in the Christ party) and a Pauline party (which took in Apollos). Few now hold this.
Most recent scholars see rivalry over teachers and their wisdom, not four doctrines. Paul's reply deals with one issue, boasting in human leaders.

settings.what: The word of the cross and God's choice of the weak
settings.to: The Corinthians, a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles, mostly of ordinary rank, as addressed in the whole of 1:10-4:21
settings.when: As the first main argument of the letter
settings.why: To show that the way God saved the world, through a crucified Messiah, overturns the standard by which the Corinthians were ranking their teachers. They themselves are the proof: God chose them as people who were not wise, powerful or noble.
settings.readers: Gentile believers who knew the value of eloquence and philosophy, and Jewish believers who knew the Scriptures Paul quotes. The chapter tells each group that its own measure of success (signs, wisdom) is not God's.

traditions.q: What kind of unity does Paul ask for in 1:10?
views: Unity is visible: one faith, one set of sacraments and one government under the bishops in communion with the successor of Peter. Vatican II teaches that the Church of Christ "subsists in" the Catholic Church while recognizing that many elements of sanctification and truth are found outside its visible structure and impel toward Catholic unity (Lumen Gentium 8).

The Orthodox Church understands itself as the one Church founded by Christ and the apostles, holding the faith handed on to them. Its unity is shown in common faith and in communion in the sacraments, with bishops and the seven ecumenical councils.

For the true unity of the church it is enough that the gospel is taught purely and the sacraments are given according to Christ's word; uniform human ceremonies are not needed (Augsburg Confession, article 7).

The universal church is invisible, made up of all the elect, and the visible church is made up of those who profess the true religion with their children; unity is shown where the Word and sacraments are rightly kept (Westminster Confession 25).

The visible church is a congregation of faithful people in which the pure Word of God is preached and the sacraments duly ministered (Thirty-Nine Articles, article 19). Anglicans have offered the Scriptures, the Nicene Creed, baptism and the Lord's Supper, and the historic episcopate as a base for reunion (the Chicago-Lambeth Quadrilateral, Lambeth Conference 1888, Resolution 11).
Unity is first spiritual: the body of Christ includes all the redeemed of all ages, and each local congregation is autonomous (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 6).

The Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths calls the Church "the body of Christ" and says each believer, "born of the Spirit, is an integral part of the general assembly and church of the firstborn" (item 10). Unity starts from that new birth shared by all believers.

title: Wisdom That Comes by the Spirit
sum: Paul reminds the Corinthians how he came to them: not with lofty speech or wisdom, but in weakness, fear and trembling, knowing nothing among them but Jesus Christ and him crucified, so that their faith would rest on God's power and not on human wisdom (2:1-5).

He then says that among the mature he does speak wisdom, God's hidden wisdom decided before the ages, which the rulers of this age did not understand or they would not have crucified the Lord of glory (2:6-8). God has revealed it through the Spirit, who knows God's depths as a person's spirit knows that person (2:9-12). The "natural" person does not accept the Spirit's gifts, but the spiritual person examines all things and has the mind of Christ (2:13-16).
readings: Read as a contrast of two kinds of people

Paul divides people into "natural" and "spiritual" and speaks of "the mature". Origen and Clement found here a deeper teaching for advanced Christians, and later groups made it a claim to inner knowledge. The traditions card shows how the churches have read the contrast.
Read as the same message seen from two sides

Many modern commentators hold that the "wisdom" of 2:6 is the cross itself, understood with the Spirit's help (2:8, 2:10). The "mature" are then all who hold to the cross, and the "natural" are those who find it foolish. There is no second, secret teaching.

views.H: In the Greek cities of the Roman East, travelling speakers advertised their "wisdom" with polished speeches and a display of proof (apodeixis). Paul's refusal of this style (2:1-5) is a refusal to enter the contest. His mention of "weakness and fear and trembling" may reflect how he arrived after the poor reception in Athens (Acts 17:32-34), or the physical weakness his critics mocked (2 Corinthians 10:10); the text does not say.
views.C: Verses 2:6-16 have been called a foreign body in the letter, and some think it is a pre-written teaching or even a later insertion (a few scholars, such as William Walker, have suggested 2:6-16 is non-Pauline). Most reject that, since the passage is tied in vocabulary and argument to chapters 1 and 3. Textually, 2:1 has two readings ("testimony" and "mystery"), and 2:4 and 2:13 have longer Byzantine forms. The origin of the quotation in 2:9 is unknown.
views.L: The chapter has three parts: a story of Paul's visit (2:1-5), an exposition of wisdom (2:6-16), and an ending that quotes Isaiah 40:13 and reaches "the mind of Christ". In 2:10-12 Paul argues by analogy (a person's spirit and the Spirit of God). The words "spirit/Spirit" (pneuma, 8 times) and "spiritual" (pneumatikos, 3 times) together occur 11 times in 2:10-16, and its opposite "natural" (psychikos) once, in 2:14.
views.J: Paul's "hidden wisdom" fits Jewish apocalyptic, where God gives knowledge of heavenly secrets by his Spirit (Daniel 2; the Dead Sea Scrolls speak of God's "mysteries"). Wisdom of Solomon 9:13-17 asks who can know God's counsel, and answers that no one can unless God gives wisdom and sends his holy spirit from above, which is close to 2:11-12. Philo contrasted the earthly man of Genesis 2:7 with the heavenly man of Genesis 1:27, and Birger Pearson argued that the Corinthians' talk of the "spiritual" and "natural" came from Hellenistic Jewish thought of that kind.
views.T: Chrysostom takes the "rulers" as human authorities, Origen as demonic powers. Basil of Caesarea used 2:10-11 to argue that the Spirit is not a creature (On the Holy Spirit 16). Clement and Origen read the "mature" as advanced believers. Luther's Small Catechism on the Third Article echoes 2:14: no one can believe by his own reason or strength. The Orthodox speak of the "mind of Christ" in connection with theosis.

deep.h: What is "the wisdom among the mature"?
deep.b:
The passage seems at first to say that Paul has a second, higher message. But look at what he says it is about. The wisdom was decided "before the ages for our glory" (2:7); the rulers failed to understand it because they crucified "the Lord of glory" (2:8); and it is revealed by the Spirit (2:10). The content, then, is God's plan of salvation through the crucified Lord, which Paul has already called "God's wisdom" in 1:24. The "mature" are not an elite; they are those who see the cross as God's wisdom.

Others read the passage differently. Some early Christian teachers, such as Clement of Alexandria and Origen, took it to show that Christians can advance from simple faith to deeper knowledge. Some second-century groups called themselves "the perfect" and used this passage to support a secret teaching, which most later writers rejected. Paul's own wording in 3:1-3 suggests that he used "mature" against the Corinthians' pride: whoever is still quarreling is not mature.

deep.h: Three Greek phrases that decide the sense
deep.b: "Natural" (psychikos, 2:14) comes from psyche, the life or soul, and names a person with only ordinary human life, without the Spirit. See the note. "Examines" (anakrino, 2:14-15) is the word for a legal hearing, and Paul uses it again in 4:3-4 for the Corinthians' examination of him. The spiritual person examines everything but is himself examined by no one, which does not mean that he cannot be corrected (compare 14:29), only that he is not answerable to an unbelieving court. "Putting spiritual things into spiritual words" (2:13) can also be read "explaining spiritual things to spiritual people" or "comparing spiritual things with spiritual things"; see the note.

echoes: Isaiah 64:4; Isaiah 65:16-17; Isaiah 40:13; Romans 11:34; Daniel 2:28; Genesis 2:7; Wisdom of Solomon 9:13-17; 1 Corinthians 1:24; 1 Corinthians 15:44-46; Colossians 2:2-3; 1 Clement 34:8; Gospel of Thomas 17

settings.what: How Paul first came to Corinth
settings.to: The Corinthians, who remembered his visit
settings.when: Recalling his first stay in the city (in the early 50s AD), seen from Ephesus a few years later
settings.why: To remind them that their faith was not produced by his skill, so that no teacher can be a ground for boasting. If their faith rested on power and not on persuasion, then it rests on God.
settings.readers: Members who may now have compared Paul's plain style with Apollos' polish. Paul tells them his weakness was by design.

settings.what: God's wisdom, revealed by the Spirit
settings.to: The Corinthians who thought themselves wise and "spiritual"
settings.when: Following his rejection of human wisdom, as a second move: that there is a true wisdom after all
settings.why: Possibly to correct the idea, if some held it, that Paul's message is simple and unlearned. There is a depth to it, but it is known only by the Spirit, and it is the same cross. The passage prepares his charge in 3:1-4 that the Corinthians, who claim to be spiritual, are acting like babies.
settings.readers: A church fond of the word "spiritual" and of "wisdom", which may have used both against Paul. Paul takes their words and fills them with his meaning.
views: God's wisdom is the saving plan centered on the crucified Lord.
The wisdom is a fuller teaching on God's plan for advanced believers (Origen, Clement).
Some commentators hear "mature" and "spiritual" as the Corinthians' own self-description, which Paul takes over and redefines around the cross.

traditions.q: Who is the "spiritual person" and who is merely "natural" (2:14-15; 3:1-3)?
views: The natural person is the unbeliever, who cannot receive spiritual things without the Spirit's work; the spiritual person is every believer who has the Spirit (Romans 8:9). The believers Paul calls "fleshly" in 3:1-3 are believers in whom the flesh still prevails; Calvin called them "babes in Christ" begotten by the Spirit, not people without grace (commentary on 3:1-3).

The natural person cannot by his own reason or strength believe in Christ or come to him; the Holy Spirit calls, enlightens and makes holy through the gospel (Luther, Small Catechism, the Third Article).
The Trinity gives the baptized sanctifying grace, enabling them to believe in God and to live under the prompting of the Holy Spirit (Catechism 1266).
Orthodox teaching describes the Christian life as growth in union with God (theosis) through the Holy Spirit, in stages often named purification, illumination and union.

Wesley described the "natural man" as asleep to God, the "legal" man as awakened but under the law, and the "evangelical" man as one who has the Spirit of adoption; being born again is what makes a person spiritual ("The Spirit of Bondage and of Adoption").

Many evangelical writers, following Lewis Sperry Chafer's He That Is Spiritual (1918), find three kinds of people in 2:14-3:3: the natural (unbeliever), the carnal or fleshly (a believer living by human ways) and the spiritual (a believer led by the Spirit). Reformed and other critics reply that Paul describes a behavior of believers, not a fixed class.

title: Servants, Builders and God's Temple
sum: Paul says he had to speak to the Corinthians as to infants, with milk and not solid food. Their jealousy and strife show that they are still living by human ways (3:1-4). Apollos and Paul are only servants: "I planted, Apollos watered, but God made it grow." The church is God's field and God's building (3:5-9).

As a master builder Paul laid a foundation, Jesus Christ, and others build on it. On the Day each builder's work will be tested by fire; what lasts earns a reward, and what burns is lost, though the builder is saved "as if through fire" (3:10-15). The church is God's temple, and whoever ruins it, God will ruin (3:16-17). So no one should boast about people: everything belongs to them, and they belong to Christ and Christ to God (3:18-23).
readings: Read as a warning to church leaders

The fire and the temple warnings fall mainly on those who teach: they build with good or poor materials and risk ruining the temple by splitting it. Many commentators read the passage this way. Ordinary members are included only as the building.
Read as a text about the afterlife

From the early church on, the fire of 3:13-15 has been linked to what happens to people after death, and early readers did not agree. Origen read it as a cleansing fire. Augustine first read the fire as the trouble of this life, and said of an afterlife fire that he did not contradict it, "because possibly it is true" (City of God 21.26). Gregory the Great taught a purifying fire for small faults before the Last Judgment. Chrysostom took the materials as a person's actions and the fire as a punishment in which the sinner remains (Homily 9 on 1 Corinthians). Calvin took the builders as teachers and the fire as the Spirit's testing of doctrine. The Catholic teaching on purgatory later built on readings like these; the Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican churches reject it, and Orthodox writers differ. See the card and the deep dive.

views.H: The pictures are drawn from the farm and the building site, familiar to a harbor city that was being built up as a colony. The "Day" and the fire come from Jewish thought about judgment. A "human court" (4:3) may point to a court day, as the Greek is "a human day"; here the Day is God's. The list in 3:22 includes "the world, life, death", recalling a Stoic boast that all things belong to the wise (Seneca, On Benefits 7.3-4), which the Corinthians may have repeated.
views.C: The textual notes affect English: 3:1 "made of flesh" or "fleshly", 3:3 "and dissensions", 3:4 "merely human" or "fleshly", 3:5 the order of names, and 3:13 "the fire itself". The main exegetical questions are whether the "temple" is the community or the individual (the Greek "you" is plural), and whether 3:15 says anything about the time between death and judgment.
views.L: Two sets of images frame the chapter: farm (3:6-9a) and building (3:9b-17), joined by the pivot sentence "God's field, God's building". The temple image (3:16-17) is a sudden turn from building to sanctuary, and the quotations of Job 5:13 and Psalm 94:11 (3:19-20) end the argument against human wisdom begun at 1:19. The chain "yours, Christ's, God's" (3:21-23) closes the whole section on the teachers.
views.J: The fire that tests resembles the refiner's fire of Malachi 3:2-3 and Zechariah 13:9, and the Jewish idea that the wicked or the half-righteous are cleansed in Gehenna for a time: the Mishnah has a year of judgment for the wicked in Gehenna (Eduyot 2:10), and in the Talmud the School of Shammai held that those in the middle go down into Gehenna and come up again, while the School of Hillel held that God's mercy tips the scale so that they do not go down (Rosh Hashanah 16b-17a). The two schools were active in the first century, but their views are written down only later, so we cannot say a reader of Paul's day knew these exact teachings. Paul does not appeal to them.
views.T: Origen read the fire as a cleansing after death. Augustine thought that something like it might be so (City of God 21.26) but did not decide. Gregory the Great (Dialogues 4.39) taught a purifying fire for small faults. Florence (1439) and Trent (1563) defined purgatory. Calvin (Institutes 3.5.6-10), the Smalcald Articles and the Thirty-Nine Articles reject it, and Orthodox churches pray for the dead but did not accept the Latin teaching (Mark of Ephesus). Chrysostom takes the materials as a person's actions. Calvin (commentary on 3:12-15) takes the builders as teachers and the fire as the Lord's testing of their doctrine.

deep.h: 3:10-17: the builder, the fire and the temple
deep.b:
What Paul says. Paul laid a foundation, Jesus Christ. Each person who builds on it should take care. The materials fall in two classes (gold, silver, precious stones; wood, hay, straw), and on "the Day" fire will show what each work is. If the work remains, there is a reward. If it burns, the builder loses it but is himself saved, "as if through fire". The fire tests the work (3:13); it does not punish the person.

Three readings of the fire. (1) The final judgment itself. The fire is a picture of the Day of Christ when every work is exposed. This is how the Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican churches read it (see the card). (2) A purifying fire after death. This is the Catholic teaching on purgatory. The Catechism (1030-1032) rests it on the Church's teaching, "certain texts of Scripture" and the prayer for the dead (it quotes 2 Maccabees 12:45-46); its text does not quote 1 Corinthians 3:15. Augustine allowed it as possible; Gregory the Great and the medieval church developed it. (3) Affliction in this life. Some interpreters take the fire as the troubles through which a believer's work is tried here and now; Augustine's first reading of the fire is of this kind (City of God 21.26). Chrysostom took the materials as a person's actions and the fire as a punishment in which the sinner remains (Homily 9). Calvin's own reading is that the builders are teachers and the fire is the Lord's testing of their doctrine.

The Orthodox position. Orthodox churches pray for the dead and believe the departed can be helped by prayer, but at Ferrara-Florence Mark of Ephesus rejected the Latin teaching of a purifying fire and of satisfaction owed by the dead. Orthodox writers have differed on the details of the state of souls after death, and some speak of a testing or cleansing of the soul without taking over the Latin teaching.

The temple. The sudden change from builders to the temple (3:16-17) turns the warning toward those who split the church. "Ruin" is the same Greek verb twice. The Corinthians together are where God's Spirit lives, as Israel had the temple. A Jewish reader would hear Ezekiel's promise that God would put his sanctuary among his people forever (Ezekiel 37:26-28).

deep.h: The Jewish side: fire after death?
deep.b: Judaism developed the idea that the dead are judged and that some are cleansed in Gehenna for a limited time. The Mishnah (Eduyot 2:10) says the judgment of the wicked in Gehenna lasts twelve months. The Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 16b-17a) records a dispute between the two schools about people who are neither wholly righteous nor wholly wicked. Beth Shammai says they go down to Gehenna, cry out and come up again, as in Zechariah 13:9. Beth Hillel says God, "abounding in kindness" (Exodus 34:6), leans toward mercy, so that they do not go down. The two schools were active in the first century, but these discussions are recorded in later writings and cannot be used to date Paul's thought. They show that the idea of a limited cleansing after death was in Jewish thought. Paul does not say this is what he means.

echoes: Jeremiah 1:10; Isaiah 5:1-7; Isaiah 28:16; Isaiah 54:11-12; Job 5:13; Psalm 94:11; Malachi 3:2-3; Zechariah 13:9; Amos 4:11; Zechariah 3:2; Ezekiel 37:26-28; 2 Maccabees 12:45-46; Matthew 16:18; Ephesians 2:20-21; 1 Corinthians 6:19; 2 Corinthians 5:10; 2 Corinthians 6:16

settings.what: Still infants: Paul and Apollos as servants
settings.to: The Corinthians, who were quarreling over Paul and Apollos
settings.when: Continuing his answer to the slogans of 1:12
settings.why: To show from their jealousy and strife that they are not as mature as they think, and to put Paul and Apollos in their place: servants with a task each, in God's field.
settings.readers: Believers who ranked Paul and Apollos. Paul tells them the two men are partners, not rivals, and the growth is God's.

settings.what: The master builder, the Day of testing and the temple
settings.to: The Corinthians, and especially those who teach or lead
settings.when: At the center of his answer about teachers
settings.why: To warn each teacher to build well on the one foundation, Christ, and to remind all that the church is God's holy temple, not to be torn apart by quarrels. The Day will show the truth about the work.
settings.readers: A church where teachers and patrons were competing for influence. The warning is serious: ruin the temple and God will ruin you.
views: The "anyone" who builds on the foundation are church teachers and leaders.
Every believer builds on the foundation with his or her own life and works (held by some interpreters; no one tradition teaches it). Calvin, by contrast, read the builders as teachers.

settings.to: The Corinthians who thought themselves wise
settings.when: Closing the first main section on wisdom and teachers
settings.why: To tell them to give up the claim of wisdom, and to see that all the teachers and everything else belong to them as members of Christ. The reason not to boast in people is that people belong to the Corinthians, not the reverse.
settings.readers: People who knew the Stoic saying that all things belong to the wise. Paul grounds the saying in Christ.

views: The Church teaches that those who die in God's grace but are not fully cleansed are purified after death so as to enter heaven. The Catechism gives the name Purgatory to "this final purification of the elect," which it calls "entirely different from the punishment of the damned," and says the Church formulated the doctrine especially at Florence and Trent (1030-1031). It appeals to "certain texts of Scripture" and to the prayer for the dead, including 2 Maccabees 12:45-46, and its text does not quote 1 Corinthians 3:15 (1031-1032).

Orthodox churches pray for the departed and believe the prayer helps them, but they do not hold the Latin teaching of a purifying fire and satisfaction owed. At Ferrara-Florence Mark of Ephesus argued against it. Orthodox writers differ on what the state of souls between death and the last judgment is like, and some speak of a testing or cleansing without taking over the Latin definition.

The Smalcald Articles (Part II, article 2) say purgatory "and every solemnity, rite, and commerce connected with it" is "nothing but a specter of the devil." They give two reasons: it conflicts with the teaching that only Christ, and not the works of men, sets souls free, and nothing has been commanded or enjoined upon us concerning the dead. The Apology of the Augsburg Confession criticizes the satisfactions, indulgences and masses tied to purgatory.

Calvin calls purgatory "a deadly device of Satan" that "makes void the cross of Christ" (Institutes 3.5.6, Beveridge translation), and reads the builders of 3:12-15 as teachers and the fire as the Lord's testing of their doctrine, not as a place after death (commentary on 3:13). The Westminster Confession says the souls of the righteous are received at death into the highest heavens, and that besides heaven and hell Scripture acknowledges no place for souls separated from their bodies (32.1).
Article 22 of the Thirty-Nine Articles calls "the Romish doctrine concerning Purgatory" a "fond thing vainly invented", with no warrant in Scripture.

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 10) says Christ will judge all people in righteousness, and that the righteous will receive their reward and dwell with the Lord. It does not mention purgatory.

title: Stewards, Fools and a Father
sum: Paul asks the Corinthians to think of him and Apollos as assistants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries. What matters in a steward is faithfulness. To him it is a small matter to be examined by the Corinthians or any human court; he does not even examine himself, because the Lord is his judge, and he will bring hidden things to light on the Day (4:1-5). He has put this in terms of himself and Apollos so the Corinthians may learn "Not beyond what is written" and stop being puffed up for one teacher against another (4:6).

Then he turns to irony: "You are already full! You are already rich! You have begun to reign without us!" (4:8). The apostles, in contrast, are on show last of all like men condemned to die, fools, weak, hungry and homeless, working with their own hands (4:9-13). He writes as a father, not to shame them, sends Timothy to remind them of his ways, and asks whether he should come with a rod or in love and gentleness (4:14-21).
readings: Read as a defense of Paul's authority

Paul answers criticism: some Corinthians were examining him and comparing him to Apollos. He appeals to the Lord's final judgment and to his role as father and founder. The chapter would then be an apostle's self-defense against a church that has outgrown him.
Read as a portrait of Christian leadership

The chapter has been read as a model for church leaders: stewards, not owners; judged by faithfulness, not success; marked by weakness and suffering; and fathers in the gospel. Its picture of the apostles on show has shaped traditions of monastic and pastoral humility.

views.H: In Roman society, status and honor were on display, and a teacher or patron was judged by success and wealth. A steward was often a slave or freed slave who managed a household, and Paul describes himself in such a role. The picture of men "sentenced to death" and a "spectacle" may recall the final act in the arena or the captives at the end of a triumph. Paul's manual work (4:12) lowered his standing among those who valued ease, and refusing Corinthian support (9:12-18) may have been a refusal of a patron's claim (one scholarly view).
views.C: The phrase in 4:6, "Not beyond what is written", has no verb and has produced many theories, including the view that it is a later note. The variant in 4:6 ("not to think beyond") is Byzantine. Many scholars hold that Paul's "I have applied these things to myself and Apollos" means he has recast a quarrel about other leaders in terms of the two of them. The unity of chapters 1-4 with the rest of the letter is rarely doubted.
views.L: Chapter 4 is the close of the first section and mirrors its start. It moves from servants and judging (4:1-5), to application (4:6-7), to a burst of irony (4:8-13) with three sets of rhetorical questions and contrasts ("we are fools, you are wise"), and ends as a father (4:14-21). Verses 4:9-13 are a list of hardships, a known form that Paul uses here and in 2 Corinthians.
views.J: "My ways in Christ" (4:17) uses a Jewish term for a pattern of life, and Paul says he teaches them "in every church". The idea of a steward faithful to his master recalls the stewards in Jesus' parables and in Genesis (Joseph over Potiphar's house). Paul's refusal to be judged by people before God's Day is also Jewish: God alone sees the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).
views.T: Augustine used 4:7 against Pelagius: everything is received, so nothing is to boast of. Orthodox churches honor the fools for Christ's sake, taking 4:10 as a calling. Catholic and Orthodox writers cite 4:15 for the spiritual fatherhood of priests, while many Protestants avoid the title. The much-argued 4:6 appears in debates on Scripture and tradition (the card).

deep.h: Judged by the Lord, not by Corinth (4:1-5)
deep.b:
Paul's three terms for himself are "assistant" (hyperetes), "steward" (oikonomos) and one who is "examined" (anakrino). A steward owns nothing; he answers to the master who put him in charge. In Corinth people were rating teachers as if they were speakers in a contest. Paul says the verdict that counts is not the church's, not a "human day" (a human court), and not his own conscience ("I am aware of nothing against myself, but I am not justified by that"). The Lord alone will judge, when he brings to light what is hidden and "praise will come to each person from God" (4:5). This is the same Day as 3:13.

The practical result is a rule for the church: "stop judging before the right time." Paul is not saying that the church should never judge; he will tell the Corinthians to judge a case of sexual immorality (5:3-5) and to settle disputes among themselves (6:1-6). He is saying they should not rank leaders on the basis of outward success.

The five Greek words have no verb, and this has produced a number of readings. (1) A reference to Scripture, or to what Paul had already written. Calvin said it can be read either way and that the choice matters little. (2) The Old Testament quotations of chapters 1-3 (1:19, 1:31, 2:9, 2:16, 3:19-20): Paul's readers are to stay within what he has just cited. (3) A copy-book saying, a schoolchild's rule not to go outside the lines. (4) A Corinthian slogan that Paul quotes. (5) A marginal note that entered the text (a conjecture some scholars have made). The phrase does not say which writings count as Scripture or exclude oral teaching, which Paul praises in 11:2. The Byzantine text adds a verb, "to think beyond what is written", which is the KJV's reading.

The phrase "I have applied" (metaschematizo, to change the form of) shows Paul used himself and Apollos as a pattern for a quarrel about other leaders, so that the Corinthians would learn from them.

deep.title: Claude's theory: 4:8-13 may answer a Corinthian reading of "all things are yours"
deep.b: If the Corinthians used "all things are yours" (3:21) as a boast, then 4:8 ("you have begun to reign without us") is the answer: Paul turns their claim into irony and then shows the apostles' life as the real pattern of Christ's reign now. On this reading 3:21-23 and 4:8-13 are two halves of one reply, and "already" in 4:8 repeats "present" in 3:22 ("things present or things to come"). This is my own suggestion. It builds on the common view that the Corinthians held an over-realized sense of the end, but the link between 3:22 and 4:8 is not something I have seen argued in this form.

echoes: 1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 9:23-24; Luke 12:42; Luke 6:28; Matthew 23:9; Romans 14:17; Romans 16:23; Acts 16:1-3; Acts 18:3; 2 Corinthians 4:7-12; 2 Corinthians 11:23-33; 1 Thessalonians 2:7-11; Philippians 2:19-22

settings.what: Servants, stewards and the apostles on show
settings.to: The Corinthians, who were examining and ranking their teachers
settings.when: As the close of the first section, with an ironic turn at 4:8
settings.why: To teach that leaders are judged by the Lord's coming Day and by faithfulness, not by the church's ranking, and to bring down the church's pride by contrasting its claim to rule with the apostles' hardships.
settings.readers: Believers who saw themselves as already rich, wise and reigning. The irony is aimed at a church that liked success.

settings.what: A father's appeal and the sending of Timothy
settings.when: At the end of the section, with Timothy about to arrive and Paul himself to follow
settings.why: To soften the sharpness of what he has said by naming himself as their father in Christ, to ask them to follow his example, to announce Timothy's visit, and to tell the puffed-up that he will test their power, not their talk.
settings.readers: A church that had many teachers but one founder. Timothy, known to them from the first visit (Acts 18:5), carries the letter's message in person.

traditions.q: Does "Not beyond what is written" (4:6) limit Christian teaching to Scripture?
views: Scripture alone is the rule of faith: the whole counsel of God is in Scripture, and nothing is to be added to it (Westminster Confession 1.6). Calvin, on 4:6, took "what is written" as Paul's own writings or the scriptural proofs he had given, and treated the choice as a small matter.
Holy Scripture is the only rule and norm by which all teachings and teachers are judged; the creeds and confessions are witnesses to what Scripture says (Formula of Concord, Epitome).
The Bible is the supreme standard by which all human conduct, creeds and religious opinions should be tried (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 1).

Holy Scripture contains all things necessary to salvation, and what is not read in it or cannot be proved by it is not to be required of anyone as an article of faith (Thirty-Nine Articles, article 6).
Scripture and sacred Tradition flow from the same divine source and are received with equal devotion; the task of interpreting both belongs to the Church's teaching office (Dei Verbum 9-10).
Scripture is the heart of Holy Tradition and is read within the Church, through the Fathers, the councils and worship.
